meta.home: I'm Lorenzo, a senior software engineer. I build web apps, internal tools, integrations and automation, usually starting from a problem rather than a spec.
meta.work: Selected work. Full-stack AI products, client platforms and a couple of things built at hackathon speed, with what was actually hard about each one.
meta.about: Senior software engineer. Frontend heavy, comfortable across the backend and architecture. How I think about building software, and what I've built.

hero.status: Open to a couple of projects
hero.lede: I'm Lorenzo. I write software for a living: web apps, APIs, internal tools. The hard part is usually working out what to build, so that's where I start.

capabilities.title: Nobody hands me a finished spec.
capabilities.lede: It's usually a description of something slow, repetitive, or held together by a spreadsheet. Working out what to build from that is most of the job. This is the kind of thing it turns into.

productsFromScratch.title: Products from nothing
productsFromScratch.body: An idea turned into something people can sign up for. Architecture, interface, API, database, deploys. AInterest is the whole thing done this way, so you can go and click around it.

internalTools.title: Internal tools
internalTools.body: The admin panel, the dashboard, the thing that finally replaces a shared spreadsheet nobody trusts. Built around how the work actually happens.

automation.title: Automating the boring parts
automation.body: The report someone assembles by hand every Monday. Data copied between two systems. Anything repetitive enough that people have stopped reading it properly.

integrations.title: Getting systems to talk
integrations.body: APIs, third-party services, an old database nobody wants to touch. Most of the work is in the failure cases, which is also what decides whether anyone trusts the output.

aiWorkflows.title: AI where it's worth it
aiWorkflows.body: I've shipped AI features to production and recorded a course on working with AI tooling. That's also why I'll tell you when a model is a worse answer than fifty lines of code.

modernisation.title: Codebases that got slow
modernisation.body: Frontend architecture, performance, structure. Usually an app that grew faster than anyone had time to plan for, where every small change now takes a week.

work.title: Things I've built.
work.lede: What each one was, and the part that turned out to be hard.
work.pageLede: Products, client work, and a couple of things built at hackathon speed. For each one I've written down the problem, what I built, and where it got difficult.

archive.title: Everything else.
archive.lede: Smaller builds, hackathon entries and old experiments. Most of them aren't maintained. They're here because this is the honest version of the list.

ainterest.summary: A full-stack AI image app with a shared feed.
ainterest.problem: Image generation tools bury everything in a chat log. You can't easily go back to what you made last week, and you never see what anyone else is doing with the same model.
ainterest.built: Prompt goes in, image comes out, and you can publish it to a feed anyone can browse. React and TypeScript on the front, a Fastify API behind it, with accounts, storage and persistence.
ainterest.challenge: Almost none of the difficulty is the model call. Generation is slow, it costs money, and it fails in ways a normal API doesn't. The interface has to be honest about that without looking broken, and the feed has to stay quick as it fills up.
ainterest.value: Talking about AI features is easy. Shipping one with accounts, storage and a UI people can actually use is the part that counts, so I did that.

nextremum.summary: A telecoms provider that had to be understandable before anyone would call.
nextremum.problem: Nextremum sells private networking and connectivity across Europe and Asia. It's a technical purchase with a lot of trust attached, and nobody starts that conversation before they understand the offer.
nextremum.built: A Next.js and TypeScript site built around services and coverage. Layouts that survive the offering growing, and pages that still read properly on a phone.
nextremum.challenge: Infrastructure copy is dense. It had to become scannable for whoever signs off on the budget without losing the detail the engineer on the call is checking for.
nextremum.value: The offer holds up whether the person reading it is buying it or specifying it.

kraanveld.summary: A crane rental company, presented like someone you'd trust with a crane.
kraanveld.problem: Renting heavy equipment is a trust decision. Before anyone picks up the phone they want to see the fleet, what you've lifted, and that this clearly isn't your first job.
kraanveld.built: Next.js and TypeScript. Services, completed projects, contact. Built so it can be updated for years instead of rebuilt in two.
kraanveld.challenge: The work is visual, so the site leans on large photography. That has to load quickly on a phone at a site with bad signal, not only on a fast connection.
kraanveld.value: Whatever gets someone to pick up the phone is the first thing on the page.

aiForFrontend.summary: An online course on using AI tooling for frontend work.
aiForFrontend.problem: Teams were adopting AI coding tools without agreeing on where they help and where they quietly cost an afternoon.
aiForFrontend.built: I designed and recorded the whole course. Curriculum, worked examples, delivery.
aiForFrontend.challenge: The tooling moves every few months, so the material had to be about how you work rather than whichever tool happened to be ahead that month.
aiForFrontend.value: Explaining AI-assisted development to other developers is a stricter test than using it yourself.

wayport.summary: Indoor airport navigation, built at hackathon speed.
wayport.problem: Airports are hard to read when you're late. Gates, services and facilities are exactly what you can't find at the moment you need them.
wayport.built: A React Native app for getting around inside an airport. Designed, built and demoed inside a hackathon.
wayport.challenge: Deciding what to cut. With a fixed deadline the only way to end up with something real is to pick the one flow that has to work and drop everything else.
wayport.value: Same instinct an MVP needs. Pick the thing that proves the idea and build that part properly.

archiveItems.cahulConnect: A city platform pulling local businesses, events and public services into one place. Built at GigaHack.
archiveItems.weather: Weather where you are, or the forecast for any city you look up.
archiveItems.pulse: A sports store template, built to get the layout fundamentals right.
archiveItems.writerWorks: A template on plain web technologies, mostly an excuse to work on animation and layout.

process.title: You talk to the person writing the code.
process.lede: Small engagements, no account manager in the middle.

understand.title: Understand the problem
understand.body: A call and a lot of questions about how the work gets done today. Fairly often the thing worth building isn't the thing that was asked for.

scope.title: Agree the smallest useful version
scope.body: What ships first, what it costs, what's deliberately left out. No open-ended discovery phase billed by the hour.

build.title: Build where you can see it
build.body: You get something you can click through while it's being built. Changing direction is cheap early and expensive late, so I'd rather hear it early.

handOver.title: Ship it and hand it over
handOver.body: Deployed, documented, yours. You shouldn't need me on a retainer to keep it running.

aboutTeaser.title: One person, start to finish.
aboutTeaser.body1: I'm Lorenzo. Senior software engineer, currently working on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, with a small number of client projects alongside it. I'm also finishing a master's at the University of Oradea.
aboutTeaser.body2: Most of my work has been frontend heavy (React, Next.js, Solid.js, Angular) but I've built and run the backend side too, mostly Fastify and Express. I use agentic tooling every day and recorded a course teaching it.
aboutTeaser.body3: In practice that means one person holding the whole thing, from the first conversation about what's going wrong to the version running in production.

contact.title: Tell me what isn't working.
contact.lede: A few sentences is enough. I'll tell you honestly whether it's worth building, and whether I'm the right person to build it.

about.title: The longer version.
about.lede: Software engineer. Currently senior, still mostly curious.
about.intro: I'm Lorenzo, a software engineer and a master's student at the University of Oradea. Day to day I work as a Senior Software Engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>.
about.freelance: On the side I take a small number of client projects and keep my own things running. That's where I try ideas out before they end up in anyone's production system.
about.career: Most of my career has been spent near the interface, React and Next.js above all. The interesting problems are rarely only frontend though. I've built APIs, designed data models, made architecture calls, and owned features from the first conversation through to deploy.
about.interests: The part I actually enjoy comes before the code, working out what should exist at all. Fast interfaces and interactions that feel right are the craft. Deciding what to build is the harder half.

principles.title: A few things I believe about building software.

problem.title: The brief is a guess
problem.body: People describe solutions because that's the vocabulary they have. My first job is finding the problem underneath and checking whether the requested solution actually solves it.

smallest.title: Ship the smallest real thing
smallest.body: A narrow version in production teaches you more than a broad version in a document. Scope is a design decision, not a negotiating position.

maintainable.title: Someone has to maintain this
maintainable.body: Clever code is a liability. I write for whoever reads it in a year, which is usually me. Structure, types, boring predictable patterns.

ai.title: AI is a tool, not a plan
ai.body: I use agentic tooling every day and taught a course on it. That's exactly why I'll say when a model is the wrong answer to your problem.

techStack.title: What I reach for.
techStack.intro: The choice follows the problem. These are the ones I know well enough to argue about.

outro.title: Away from the screen.
outro.body: I read more JavaScript newsletters than is reasonable, and spend a fair amount of time on creative coding, which has no business case whatsoever. That's mostly the appeal.
